# 1. Overview

Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) is a spatial statistical method that models local relationships between non-stationary environmental or demographic variables and a specific outcome. In this exercise, you will use GWR to build hedonic pricing models that analyze how structural and locational factors influenced condominium resale prices in 2015.

## The data

Two data sets will be used in this model building exercise, they are:

- URA Master Plan subzone boundary in shapefile format (i.e. *MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL*)

- condo_resale_2015 in csv format (i.e. *condo_resale_2015.csv*)

## The tools

In this exercise, we use below R package to do analysis.

- R package for building OLS and performing diagnostics tests

  - [**olsrr**](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/)

- R package for calibrating geographical weighted family of models

  - [**GWmodel**](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GWmodel/index.html)

- R package for multivariate data visualisation and analysis

  - [**corrplot**](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/corrplot/vignettes/corrplot-intro.html)

- Spatial data handling

  - **sf**

- Attribute data handling

  - **tidyverse**, especially **readr**, **ggplot2** and **dplyr**

- Choropleth mapping

  - **tmap**.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(olsrr, corrplot, ggpubr, ggplot2,
               sf, sfdep, GWmodel, tmap, 
               tidyverse, gtsummary,
               performance, RColorBrewer)
```

::: callout-note
The `GWmodel` package offers a suite of localized spatial statistical tools, including geographically weighted (GW) summary statistics, principal components analysis, discriminant analysis, and several regression models in both standard and outlier-resistant formats. Mapping the results of these models serves as a valuable exploratory step that often guides more advanced or traditional statistical analyses.
:::

# 2. Data preparation

## 2.1 Importing geospatial data

This exercise uses the MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL geospatial dataset, an ESRI shapefile containing polygon features that represent the URA Master Plan 2014 planning subzone boundaries. The GIS data is mapped using the SVY21 projected coordinate system.

```{r}
mpsz = st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", 
               layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL")
```

## 2.2 Updating CRS information

The report indicates that the imported MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL shapefile is stored in R as a simple feature object named `mpsz`, utilizing a multipolygon geometry. Crucially, this spatial object is currently missing its EPSG coordinate reference system information.

Import town geospatial data

```{r}
mpsz_svy21 <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
```

Verify the projection of the newly transformed *mpsz_svy21* by using `st_crs()` of **sf** package.

```{r}
st_crs(mpsz_svy21)

```

Reveal the extent of *mpsz_svy21* by using `st_bbox()` of sf package.

```{r}
st_bbox(mpsz_svy21)
```

## 2.3 Importing asspatial data

The *condo_resale_2015* is in csv file format. The codes chunk below uses `read_csv()` function of **readr** package to import *condo_resale_2015* into R as a tibble data frame called *condo_resale*.

```{r}
condo_resale = read_csv("data/aspatial/Condo_resale_2015.csv")
```

Verify store data

```{r}
glimpse(condo_resale)
```

```{r}
head(condo_resale$LONGITUDE)
```

The print above reveals that the values of *LONGITITUDE* and *LATITUDE* fields are in decimal degree. Most probably wgs84 geographic coordinate system is used.

Next, `summary()` of base R is used to display the summary statistics of *cond_resale* tibble data frame.

```{r}
summary(condo_resale)
```

## 2.4 Converting aspatial data frame into a sf object

The `condo_resale` tibble is currently an aspatial data frame. The following code chunk uses the `st_as_sf()` function from the `sf` package to convert it into a spatial simple feature object.

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- st_as_sf(condo_resale,
                            coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"),
                            crs=4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs=3414)
```

verify data

```{r}
head(condo_resale.sf)
```

# 3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

## 3.1 EDA using statistical graphics

Plot the distribution of *SELLING_PRICE* by using appropriate Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

```{r}
# Generate the plot
ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf, aes(x=`SELLING_PRICE`)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

```

The figure above reveals a right skewed distribution. This means that more condominium units were transacted at relative lower prices.

Statistically, the skewed dsitribution can be normalised by using log transformation. The code chunk below is used to derive a new variable called *LOG_SELLING_PRICE* by using a log transformation on the variable *SELLING_PRICE*. It is performed using `mutate()` of **dplyr** package.

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(`LOG_SELLING_PRICE` = log(SELLING_PRICE))
```

plot the *LOG_SELLING_PRICE*

```{r}
ggplot(data=condo_resale.sf, 
       aes(x=`LOG_SELLING_PRICE`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")
```

Distribution is less skewed now.

# 4. Hedonic Pricing Modelling in R

building hedonic pricing models for condominium resale units using [`lm()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.5.2/topics/lm) of R base.

## 4.1 Simple Linear Regression Method

Build a simple linear regression model by using *SELLING_PRICE* as the dependent variable and *AREA_SQM* as the independent variable.

```{r}
condo.slr <- lm(formula=SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM, 
                data = condo_resale.sf)
```

The `lm()` function outputs a model object classified as "lm", or "mlm" when handling multiple responses. You can evaluate these results using `summary()` for a detailed statistical overview and `anova()` for an analysis of variance table. Additionally, generic accessor functions like `coefficients()`, `effects()`, `fitted.values()`, and `residuals()` allow you to easily extract specific elements from the fitted model.

```{r}
summary(condo.slr)
```

The report indicates that the simple linear regression model, expressed as

*y = -258121.1 + 14719x1*

accounts for approximately 45% of the variation in selling prices.

Highly significant p-values for both the overall model and its individual coefficients (intercept and area) confirm that this regression is a statistically valid estimator that outperforms a simple mean.

Furthermore, we can visualize this relationship by mapping the `lm()` method directly onto a ggplot scatterplot to display the line of best fit.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
ggplot(data=condo_resale.sf,  
       aes(x=`AREA_SQM`, y=`SELLING_PRICE`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm)
```

Figure above reveals that there are a few statistical outliers with relatively high selling prices.

## 4.2 Multiple Linear Regression Method

Prior to developing a multiple regression model, we must ensure that your independent variables are not heavily correlated with one another. Including highly correlated predictors compromises the reliability and quality of the model, a statistical issue known as multicollinearity.

A correlation matrix is an effective tool for visualizing pairwise relationships between independent variables. While base R provides the `pairs()` function, specialized packages such as `corrplot` offer cleaner, more informative displays. The following code chunk uses `corrplot` to generate a correlation matrix illustrating how the predictors in the `condo_resale` dataset interact.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10
corrplot(cor(condo_resale[, 5:23]), 
         diag = FALSE, 
         order = "AOE",
         tl.pos = "td", 
         tl.cex = 0.5, 
         method = "number", 
         type = "upper")
```

Reordering a correlation matrix is essential for uncovering hidden structures and patterns within the data. The `corrplot` package provides four reordering algorithms via the `order` parameter: `"AOE"`, `"FPC"`, `"hclust"`, and `"alphabet"`. Here, the `"AOE"` (Angular Order of the Eigenvectors) method is applied to arrange the variables based on their eigenvector angles.

From the scatterplot matrix, it is clear that ***Freehold*** is highly correlated to ***LEASE_99YEAR***. In view of this, it is wiser to only include either one of them in the subsequent model building. As a result, ***LEASE_99YEAR*** is excluded in the subsequent model building.

## 4.3 Building a hedonic pricing model using multiple linear regression method

calibrate the multiple linear regression model.

```{r}
condo.mlr <- lm(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_HAWKER_MARKET   +
    PROX_KINDERGARTEN   + PROX_MRT  + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH +
    PROX_SHOPPING_MALL  + PROX_SUPERMARKET + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + 
    FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.mlr)
```

::: callout-note
This multiple linear regression model explains **64.7% of the variance** in condominium resale prices (Adjusted $R^2 = 0.6474$, $p < 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$).

### Key Highlights

- **Overall Model Fit:** The high $F$-statistic (147.4, $p < 0.001$) indicates the combined set of structural and locational predictors is statistically significant.

- **Primary Structural Drivers:**

  - **Unit Size (`AREA_SQM`):** Strongest positive driver ($t = 34.39$), adding approximately **+\$12,708** per additional square meter ($p < 0.001$).

  - **Tenure (`FREEHOLD`):** Commands a premium of roughly **+\$359,913** over leasehold ($p < 0.001$).

  - **Age (`AGE`):** Each additional year reduces price by about **-\$24,441** ($p < 0.001$).

  - **Development Size (`NO_Of_UNITS`):** Slight negative relationship (about -\$231 per unit, $p = 0.0095$).

- **Locational Drivers (Accessibility):**

  - Greater distance to key amenities reduces prices as expected: **CBD** (-\$78,670/km), **MRT** (-\$314,600/km), **Shopping Malls** (-\$206,604/km), and **Childcare** (-\$351,618/km).

  - Positive coefficients on variables like **`PROX_PARK`** and **`PROX_BUS_STOP`** suggest homes further away sold for more in this global model—a classic indicator of omitted spatial correlation or spatial non-stationarity that Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) is designed to resolve.

- **Non-Significant Predictors:** Proximity to **Hawker Markets** ($p = 0.418$), **Supermarkets** ($p = 0.560$), and **Top Primary Schools** ($p = 0.911$) do not show statistically significant relationships at the 5% level in this global specification.
:::

## 4.4 Revising the model

Based on the regression report, several independent variables are not statistically significant. We can refine the model by dropping these non-significant predictors and recalibrating it using the code chunk below.

```{r}
condo.mlr1 <- lm(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_MRT +
    PROX_ELDERLYCARE    + PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA +
    PROX_PARK   + PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + 
    PROX_SHOPPING_MALL  + PROX_BUS_STOP + 
    NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data=condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.mlr1)

```

The output above reveals that all explanatory variables are statistically significant at 95% confident level.

::: callout-note
This revised model achieves virtually identical explanatory power (**Adjusted** $R^2 = 0.6472$) while eliminating the four non-significant predictors, resulting in a more parsimonious specification with a higher overall $F$-statistic (**189.1**, $p < 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$).

Every remaining predictor is now statistically significant at the 1% level ($p < 0.01$) or better ($p < 0.001$).
:::

**Locational Predictors:**

- Expected proximity premiums persist for **CBD** (-\$77,131/km), **MRT** (-\$294,745/km), **Shopping Malls** (-\$220,947/km), and **Childcare** (-\$318,473/km).

- Positive distance coefficients for **`PROX_PARK`**, **`PROX_BUS_STOP`**, and **`PROX_ELDERLYCARE`** remain prominent, highlighting persistent local spatial non-stationarity that global OLS cannot decouple.

## 4.5 Preparing Publication Quality Table: gtsummary method

The `gtsummary` package offers a flexible, elegant toolset for generating publication-ready summary tables in R. The following code chunk uses `tbl_regression()` to produce a cleanly formatted regression report.

```{r}
tbl_regression(condo.mlr1, intercept = TRUE)
```

Using the `gtsummary` package, you can incorporate overall model statistics into your report either by appending them directly to the table using `add_glance_table()` or by displaying them as a footnote using `add_glance_source_note()`, as demonstrated in the code chunk below.

```{r}
tbl_regression(condo.mlr1, 
               intercept = TRUE) %>% 
  add_glance_source_note(
    label = list(sigma ~ "\U03C3"),
    include = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, 
                AIC, statistic,
                p.value, sigma))
```

## 4.6 Regression Diagnostics

Regression diagnostics are essential procedures for evaluating whether an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) model satisfies its underlying statistical assumptions and genuinely fits the underlying data. These checks test for non-linearity, non-normal errors, heteroskedasticity (non-constant variance), and influential outliers to ensure that parameter estimates and inferences remain valid and reliable. Common approaches combine graphical inspections—such as residual and Q-Q plots—with formal quantitative tests.

In R, the `olsrr` package is specifically designed to streamline these evaluations. It provides an extensive toolkit for diagnosing and refining multiple linear regression models, including:

- Comprehensive regression output summaries

- Residual diagnostics and normality checks

- Measures of influence and outlier detection

- Heteroskedasticity tests

- Collinearity diagnostics

- Overall model fit assessment

- Predictor contribution evaluations

- Automated variable selection algorithms

### 4.6.1 Multicollinearity test

Multicollinearity arises when predictor variables share strong linear relationships, preventing the model from isolating each factor's independent effect on the outcome. Testing for multicollinearity is vital in multiple linear regression: high correlation among predictors inflates the variance of coefficient estimates, making them volatile, difficult to interpret, and prone to type II errors (masking truly significant variables).

The following code chunk uses the `check_collinearity()` function from the `performance` package to evaluate the model for potential multicollinearity issues.

```{r}
# Check for Multicollinearity
check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)
```

```{r}
mlr.vif <- check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)
plot(mlr.vif)
```

Since the VIF of the independent variables are less than 10. We can safely conclude that there are no sign of multicollinearity among the independent variables.

### 4.6.2 Test for Non-Linearity

In multiple linear regression, validating the core assumptions of linearity and additivity between the dependent and independent variables is essential. The following code chunk uses `ols_plot_resid_fit()` from the `olsrr` package to generate a residuals-versus-fitted values plot to test this linearity assumption.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(see)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
check_model(condo.mlr1,
            check = "linearity")
```

The figure above reveals that most of the data poitns are scattered around the 0 line, hence we can safely conclude that the relationships between the dependent variable and independent variables are linear.

### 4.6.3 Test for Normality Assumption

The normality assumption test in multiple linear regression evaluates whether the model residuals—the discrepancies between observed and predicted values—follow a normal distribution. Satisfying this assumption is essential for valid confidence intervals and reliable hypothesis testing. Residual normality can be assessed visually through histograms and quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plots, or quantitatively using formal hypothesis tests such as the Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests.

The code chunk below employs `check_normality()` from the `performance` package to evaluate the normality of the residuals for the `condo.mlr1` model.

```{r}
check_normality(condo.mlr1)
```

```         
Warning: Non-normality of residuals detected (p < .001).
```

The print above reveals that the p-value of the normality assumption test is less than alpha value of 0.05. Hence we reject the normality assumption at 95% confident level.

Instead of showing the test statistic, `plot()` of **see** package can be used to plot a the output of `check_normality()` for visual inspection as shown below.

```{r}
plot(check_normality(condo.mlr1), 
     type = "qq")
```

Q-Q plot above below shows that majority of the data points are felt along the zero line.

Another way to check for normality assumption visual is by using [`check_model()`](https://easystats.github.io/performance/reference/check_model.html) of performance package.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
check_model(condo.mlr1,
            check= "normality")
```

The figure reveals that the residual of the multiple linear regression model (i.e. condo.mlr1) is resemble normal distribution.

### 4.6.4 Testing for Spatial Autocorrelation

Because our hedonic pricing model relies on geographically referenced data, testing for spatial autocorrelation is essential. Traditional Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression assumes independent observations—an assumption frequently violated by spatial data, in accordance with Tobler’s First Law of Geography: *"Everything is related to everything else, but nearby things are more related than distant things."*

Spatial autocorrelation measures the degree to which a variable correlates with itself across space, manifesting as positive clustering (similar values near one another) or negative dispersion (dissimilar neighbors). Overlooking this spatial dependency causes critical modeling issues:

- **Biased standard errors & inflated Type I errors:** Artificially deflated standard errors distort $t$-statistics and $p$-values, making predictors appear spuriously significant.

- **Misleading significance tests:** Standard models conflate true explanatory relationships with underlying spatial clustering.

- **Model misspecification:** Spatial patterning in the residuals indicates omitted spatial variables or unmodeled spatial processes.

A Moran’s $I$ test evaluated on regression residuals diagnoses this issue: statistically significant residual autocorrelation confirms that global OLS fails to capture the spatial structure. To execute this test, we must first extract the residuals from our hedonic pricing model and bind them to our spatial data frame.

```{r}
mlr.output <- as.data.frame(condo.mlr1$residuals)
```

Next, we will join the newly created data frame with *condo_resale.sf* object.

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- cbind(condo_resale.sf, 
                         condo.mlr1$residuals) %>%
  rename(`MLR_RES` = `condo.mlr1.residuals`)

```

Next, we will use **tmap** package to display the distribution of the residuals on an interactive map.

```{r}
tmap_mode("view")
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
#tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.4) +
  tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +  
  tm_dots(
    fill = "MLR_RES",
    size = 0.7,
    col = "black",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(
      n = 10,
      values = rev(
        brewer.pal(11, "RdBu")),
      style = "quantile",
      midpoint = NA),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residuals")
  ) + 
  tm_title("LM Residuals (Quantile Classification)") +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11,14))
```

```{r}
tmap_mode("plot")
```

The figure highlights observable patterns of spatial autocorrelation. To formally verify this visual evidence, we will conduct a Global Moran’s $I$ test.

We begin by constructing a distance-based spatial weights matrix using the `st_dist_band()` function from the `sfdep` package.

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>% 
  mutate(
    nb = st_dist_band(
      st_geometry(geometry), 
      upper = 1500),
    wt = st_weights(
      nb, style = "W"),
    .before = 1) 
```

Next, [`global_moran_perm()`](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/reference/global_moran_perm) of **sfdep** package will be used to perform Moran’s I test for residual spatial autocorrelation.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(
  condo_resale.sf$MLR_RES, 
  nb = condo_resale.sf$nb, 
  wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
  alternative = "two.sided", 
  nsim = 499)
```

The Global Moran’s I test for residual spatial autocorrelation shows that it’s p-value is less than 0.00000000000000022 which is less than the alpha value of 0.05. Hence, we will reject the null hypothesis that the residuals are randomly distributed.

Since the Observed Global Moran I = 0.14389 which is greater than 0, we can infer than the residuals resemble cluster distribution.

# 5. Building Hedonic Pricing Models using GWmodel

In this section, we are going to learn how to modelling hedonic pricing using both the fixed and adaptive bandwidth schemes

## 5.1 Building Fixed Bandwidth GWR Model

### 5.1.1 Computing fixed bandwidth

In the code chunk below, `bw.gwr()` from the `GWmodel` package is used to determine the optimal fixed bandwidth for the model. Setting the argument `adaptive = FALSE` specifies that a fixed spatial distance bandwidth should be calculated rather than an adaptive neighbor count.

To determine the stopping criterion, two optimization approaches are available: Cross-Validation (`"CV"`) and Corrected Akaike Information Criterion (`"AIC"` or `"AICc"`). The stopping rule is specified via the `approach` argument.

```{r}
bw.fixed <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE    +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL   + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + 
    FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  approach="CV", 
  kernel="gaussian", 
  adaptive=FALSE, 
  longlat=FALSE)
```

The result shows that the recommended bandwidth is 971.3405 metres. (Quiz: Do you know why it is in metre?)

### 5.1.2 GWModel method - fixed bandwith

calibrate the gwr model using fixed bandwidth and gaussian kernel.

```{r}
gwr.fixed <- gwr.basic(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE    +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL   + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + 
    FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  bw=bw.fixed, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  longlat = FALSE)
```

The output is saved in a list of class “gwrm”. The code below can be used to display the model output.

```{r}
gwr.fixed
```

The report shows that the AICc of the gwr is 42263.61 which is significantly smaller than the globel multiple linear regression model of 42967.1.

## 5.2 Building Adaptive Bandwidth GWR Model

In this section, we will calibrate the gwr-based hedonic pricing model by using adaptive bandwidth approach.

### 5.2.1 Computing the adaptive bandwidth

Similar to the earlier section, we will first use `bw.gwr()` to determine the recommended data point to use.

The code chunk used look very similar to the one used to compute the fixed bandwidth except the `adaptive` argument has changed to **TRUE**.

```{r}
bw.adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE  + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE    +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL   + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP   + NO_Of_UNITS + 
    FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD, 
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  approach="CV", 
  kernel="gaussian", 
  adaptive=TRUE, 
  longlat=FALSE)
```

The result shows that the 30 is the recommended data points to be used.

### 5.2.2 Constructing the adaptive bandwidth gwr model

Now, we can go ahead to calibrate the gwr-based hedonic pricing model by using adaptive bandwidth and gaussian kernel as shown in the code chunk below.

```{r}
gwr.adaptive <- gwr.basic(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_BUS_STOP +
    NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data=condo_resale.sf, 
  bw=bw.adaptive, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  adaptive=TRUE, 
  longlat = FALSE)
```

The code below can be used to display the model output.

```{r}
gwr.adaptive
```

The report shows that the AICc the adaptive distance gwr is 41982.22 which is even smaller than the AICc of the fixed distance gwr of 42263.61.

## 5.3 Visualising GWR Output

Beyond standard regression residuals, the output spatial feature class table provides diagnostic metrics, local parameters, and fitted values for each observation point:

- **Condition Number (`cond`):** Evaluates local multicollinearity. Values exceeding **30** indicate severe local collinearity, rendering the corresponding local coefficient estimates unstable and unreliable.

- **Local** $R^2$: Ranges from **0.0 to 1.0**, reflecting the local explanatory power of the model. Mapping Local $R^2$ highlights geographic disparities where the model performs strongly versus areas where low values signal potential omitted variables.

- **Predicted Values:** The local fitted values ($\hat{y}$) computed for each observation by the GWR model.

- **Residuals:** Calculated as observed minus predicted values ($y - \hat{y}$). Standardizing these residuals (mean = 0, standard deviation = 1) allows for diverging cold-to-hot choropleth mapping to reveal spatial clustering of over- and under-predictions.

- **Coefficient Standard Errors:** Quantify the estimation precision for each predictor. Lower standard errors relative to estimate sizes reflect higher confidence, whereas inflated errors typically point to local collinearity issues.

All of these attributes—including coordinates (`fit.points`), local parameter estimates, fitted values, standard errors, and local $t$-values—are accessible within the `@data` slot of the `SDF` (`SpatialPointsDataFrame` or `SpatialPolygonsDataFrame`) object returned in the GWR model output.

## 5.4 Converting SDF into sf data.frame
